Sustainable webdesign refers to practices and principles aimed at creating websites that minimize environmental impact. The goal is to reduce the energy consumption and carbon footprint associated with the development, hosting, and use of websites. Some key aspects of sustainable webdesign are efficient coding, optimization, green hosting, reduced data transfer, longevity and
. Even something as simple as a dark mode for the interface of an app can reduce the amount of strain on the battery of a smartphone or tablet, thus reducing energy consumption.

Many people assume that websites already are sustainable publishing format, but this is not exactly the case. Every website that’s online is hosted on a server. When you access the site, the web browser requests the file from the server and sends it back to the browser. Even if this process usually proceeds so quickly that we hardly notice it, it produces CO₂.
The carbon footprint of a website is multilayered, but one way of thinking about it is that intentional, lighter weight websites are quicker to load, and therefore less wasteful.

»Just as it’s an architect’s responsibility to think about the carbon cost of the things they design, it should be every digital designer’s responsibility to think about the same thing for the websites and apps they make.«
The digital industry is responsible for 2-5% of global emissions, more than the aviation industry. If the Internet were a country it would be one of the top five polluters. That is why in 2023 the

, which explain how to design and implement digital products and services that put people and the planet first. This guidelines provide best practices and recommendations for reducing the environmental impact of web development and design, such as minimizing data transfer, optimizing images or using green hosting.

Even though sustainable web design is a rather young concept, which has become increasingly known in recent years, the concept of sustainable design in general is not new. In architecture sustainable design gained importance during the 1960s and 70s, with the rise of the environmental movement. Architects like Buckminster Fuller paved the way for a new era of sustainable design, emphasizing the importance of energy efficiency, renewable materials, and holistic design approaches. In the decades that followed, sustainable design principles became increasingly mainstream, and today they are considered an essential component of any modern building project.

But of course not only in webdesign and architecture sustainability is an important aspect of the design process. Other disciplines like product design, fashion design or graphic design also came up with different approaches on minimizing their environmental impact.

Creative Coding refers to a process of exploration, iteration and reflection that uses code as the primary medium or tool to create artwork. In this way, creative coders engage in creative dialogue with the computer through the use of a programming language.

Creative Coding and generative design are often treated as synonymous, but they actually refer to different practices. While creative coding is linked to a computer as a tool, generative design is a method that is independent of technology and has been used for centuries in architecture, art and graphic design. The focus here is on the development of autonomous systems, rules or algorithms that serve the basis for the creation of media in the broadest sense. Representatives of this style or working method include Karl Gerstner, Gottfried Jäger, Manfred Mohr and Karl Martin Holzhäuser. Creative Coding, on the other hand, refers to a process based on the playful discovery and exploration of the possibilities of code, without pursuing a predefined goal.

The Artificial Flatness as a cultural technique is a theoretical concept by media theoretician Sybille Krämer. The study focuses on the visualization of thoughts, through which new cognition is created.

»Not only recent non-cognitivist theories of mind, but also a remarkable philosophical tradition assumes that thinking and cognition become possible in the first place because »things of thought« and »things of thought« are objectified in our external world, where they are sensually and operatively accessible.«

This refers, for example, to geographical maps or book pages, which are fundamentally based on text and image, but also to calculating by hand, beads, or by using calculating stones. The Artificial Flatness influences the way in which actions are conducted, such as finding one's way around by means of maps or solving arithmetic problems. But the surface also opens up a space for creativity. With this cultural technique, Krämer defines a special space »that can be surveyed, controlled, and manipulated in a bird's-eye view. In the two-dimensionality of the graphic, everything can be recorded: That which is, that which is not yet, and that which can never be (impossible objects).«
This clearly illustrates the context of the design profession's creative process.

Sybille Krämer's concept can also be projected onto digital screens of various display devices. However, this raises the question of multidimensionality. Does the three-dimensional, technical object on a flat display imitate an infinite, three-dimensional space? Since the development of computers, we have been talking about

The term digital literature refers to texts that are produced through and with digital media. This means that the writing process is conceptually understood in digital terms. The Internet, social networks or algorithms, for example, can serve as tools for generating texts. This clearly distinguishes digital literature from digitised literature, such as the idea of the eBook format or hypertext literature, a small movement in the early 2000s. The term was mainly coined by Hannes Bajohr, other representatives of the movement are Gregor Weichbrodt, Jörg Piringer, Kenneth Goldsmith or Andreas Bülhoff. Christiane Frohmann, Stephan Porombka and Annette Gilbert also participate in the discourse on digital literature.

»Digital literature is different from digitised literature. One can translate between the digital and the analogue, but every translation is loss and enrichment, interpretation and falsification. Just as every medium creates its own reality, the digital also creates its reality. The digital has a different reality than the analogue. Digital literature is something in which the change in the perception of the world through the digital finds representation at all. For where the digital produces other realities, it also produces other experiences. But because the text in the digital cannot only provide descriptions, but is also action, these experiences can express themselves not only descriptively, but also performatively. A text in which characters use computers is not a digital text. A digitally produced text that reflects its conditions of production is.«

Cyberfeminism is a feminist approach that focuses on the relationship between cyberspace, the Internet, and technology. The term can refer to a philosophy, methodology, or community and is used to describe feminist practices that seek to theorize, critique, explore, and reshape the Internet, cyberspace, and new media technologies in general.

The term is strongly associated with western net art of the 1990s and changed over time. Today, the term technofeminism is more often used. Technofeminism increasingly deals with activist intersections of feminism and technology.

The term cyberfeminism was coined in 1994 by Sadie Plant, director of the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit at the University of Warwick in the United Kingdom. The term is closely associated with Donna Haraway's cyborg manifesto, poststructuralist feminism, riot grrrl culture, and feminist critiques of the alleged erasure of women in discussions of technology. Although women have been actively involved in the development of new technologies throughout history, cyberfeminists have argued that technology is still seen as a male creation. Some of them argued that technology must always be questioned and reconceptualized.

In order to get to know a new medium quickly and to be able to assess its possibilities better, the use of metaphors can be a helpful tool. For example, the metaphor of the page, which is deeply rooted in the Web, or other references to the book were useful in the 1990s to help web users get started with this new medium. However, such a juxtaposition also brings with it problematic issues, because the Web is in fact not just a digital book format, but a mixed medium that combines diverse media formats and thus enables entirely new experiences and interactions. However, these can quickly be forgotten by comparison with the printed book. This can be seen, for example, in what used to be the early years of the web, when many companies merely embedded their print materials as PDFs on their websites, thereby exploiting very few of the web's possibilities. To this day, the metaphor of the page is deeply embedded in the design of websites and, as a result, still influences the way many designers conceive web projects.

Similar to the page metaphor, there is usually no change in the design process according to the different media. It is therefore not surprising that currently most websites still reflect this design process, which originated in print, in their design.

Today, there are many terms to describe the design of digital interfaces, such as screen design, webdesign, user interface (UI) design, user experience (UX) design, interaction design or digital design. However, these are often incorrectly used synonymously and are therefore difficult to distinguish from each other.

UI and UX are often regarded as separate disciplines, but in practice it is difficult to separate them. This is because the experience and user-friendliness of an interface are directly related to its design. In principle, screen design refers to the same thing as interface design, namely the graphic implementation of interfaces with the aid of a suitable layout. Strictly speaking, the function of the graphic user interface is not included here, but as in graphic design, the form can only be separated from the function with difficulty, or ideally should not be separated at all. Experience and interaction design are also two different terms for the same thing: the development of human-machine interfaces, which are as easily understood as possible. The field of usability includes a variety of aspects such as the psychology of perception, cognition, semantics, usability, ergonomics and quality of experience. However, such an interface does not necessarily have to be visual, but a purely voice-controlled interaction is also possible, for example.

Although UI and UX can be considered subcategories of webdesign, websites are no longer the only digital interfaces that need to be conceived and designed. This is why UI, UX, screen design and interaction design today usually also include the design of apps and applications for a wide variety of end devices such as televisions, smartphones, smart home devices, wearables and many more. Here, interface design plays an important role as a key factor for the acceptance of increasingly complex products that are integrated into systems. The term digital design is also increasingly used today to refer to the development of digital content of all kinds.

The term webdesign is rarely used today because it does not include the design of interfaces outside the browser. But the special thing about webdesign is that in the early years of the web it not only referred to the visual design and conception of websites, but also included the implementation through code. This is why we prefer to use the term webdesign on this website.

The term usability refers to the functional relationship between people and the products and systems they use. The idea is quite simple: if something is able to fulfil its intended function (if it is

Jakob Nielsen, one of the best-known Human Computer Interaction (HCI) experts, argued in 2000 that users visit websites because of their content. Design, in his opinion, only fulfills the task of making content as easily accessible as possible for users. Good or successful design should be transparent in order to not disturb the content. Because websites are meant to provide information, not pleasure. Their design should be as simple and clear as possible. That is why good usability has become one of the most important points for successful design. After all, usability contributes significantly to the experience of a website. Donald Norman, who became the head of Apple's research group in 1993 and later founded the Nielsen Norman Group together with Jakob Nielsen, introduced the term Experience Design in 1993. Jakob Nielsen and Donald Norman were instrumental in coining the theory that web design, or UX design, provides the best usability, when it makes interfaces and the technology behind them invisible.

This idea can be traced back to previous developments of other focal points within the design discipline that had established themselves at the beginning of the 20th century. Styles such as Bauhaus, de Stijl or International Style had in common that they strived for a clarity of form and a kind of transparency. In his manifesto »Elementare Typography« Tschichold called for a new typography that was purposeful and clearly legible and thus as pure as possible to represent the content of the text. He also argued against any form of ornamentation and other decorative elements and called on all printed matter to standardise DIN formats. Therefore, the striving for transparency of some interface designers can be traced back to Tschichold and other modernists.

A spatial interface is either a 3D interface in the field of virtual reality and augmented reality or a 2D interface that displays an apparently spatial surface and uses real objects as a metaphor to describe properties and interaction possibilities. They can orientate themselves through this system and navigate within the interface because they can locate objects and establish environmental references. The origin of this concept lies in the assumption that people have an innate sense of space, which designers can use to make the behaviour of elements inside an interface  predictable and therefore intuitively usable. The new order of the Internet, in which everything can be linked to everything else, can be understood as a methaphor of the rhizome – a postmodern or poststructuralist model developed by the two philosophers Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, which is based on non-hierarchical structures.
»A rhizome has no beginning or end; it is always in the middle, between things, interbeing, intermezzo. The tree is filiation, but the rhizome is alliance, uniquely alliance.«

The idea of the rhizome is a structural metaphor from botany and describes underground continuous growing roots that establish connections with other sprouts. A fundamental aspect of the symbol is that any point of the rhizome can be connected to any other point at any time.

Using the name of the Internet as a network or web, a structure is implied by definition in which any other point can be connected to any other point. Wherever users are and call up a URL in the browser, the link to the hyperspace is created and thus a new connection is established among billions of other already existing connections. Every single page on the Internet is just a few clicks away from every other page. The Internet, as a space of multiple multiplicities, in constant growth and change, is constantly forming new connections. Even when links and connections are broken or deleted, a new infinite number of interlocking nodes can emerge because there is no central point. Within a rhizome, new connections are constantly being made between elements – its elements are changeable, separable, connectable and reversible. These connections are made possible by servers that exist in several different locations around the world and are interconnected in a continuous manner, also creating new connections among themselves. It becomes clear that the nonlinear structure of the Internet is not only a rhizome, it also reproduces a rhizome.

The composer of electronic music Kim Cascone, as well as the researchers, artists and editors Alessandro Ludovico and Demian Conrad also use the term in their work. Hypertext, by enabling the creation of a functional, entirely new text structure in digital space, has potentially changed the linearity of text forever. The term was coined by Theodor H. Nelson in the 1960s and refers to a form of electronic text that enables non-sequential writing and reading.

In general, hypertext is defined as a unit of text, images and data linked via hyperlinks to form an overall text. This means that it has a dynamic, non-linear structure that breaks up the linear sequentiality of classic print publications. Texts therefore have no predefined reading order and contain cross-references called hyperlinks that lead to other texts or content of any form.  Through links, the interconnected content inevitably enters into a relationship with each other and opens up space for discourse.

The hypertext thus has no unity like conventional texts and can be described more as a text collection or hypertextual text structure. This allows not only a variety of reading possibilities, but also possibilities of interpretation.

Classically, hypertext is written in mark-up languages such as HTML, which are not primarily visible to the reader, but can be viewed in the browser using developer tools. The term hypertext is also often used as a synonym for hypermedia, which extends the factor of non-linearity by that of multimedia.
in hypertext by including visual information, sound, animation and other forms of data. Hypertext thus refers to an information medium that combines verbal and non-verbal information.
The postmodern philosophical concept of the
, which derives from the root system of the plant rhizome, is often used to describe the structure of hypertext.

The hypertext, and in particular its characteristic of the non-linearity of text, was euphorically welcomed by many representatives of postmodern and poststructuralist currents. The new technology was seen as a confirmation of the postmodern literary theory popular in the 1980s, which can be traced back to the ideas of Barthes, Foucault, Lyotard, Derrida, Deleuze and Guattari.

, Roland Barthes described in 1973 an ideal textuality that corresponds pretty much to what is now called hypertext. This textuality consists of blocks of words (or images) that are electronically connected by a multitude of paths, chains or trails in an open, eternally unfinished textuality.

»In this ideal text, the networks are many and interact, without any one of them being able to surpass the rest; this text is a galaxy of signifiers, not a structure of signifieds; it has no beginning; it is reversible; we gain access to it by several entrances, none of which can be authoritatively declared to be the main one; the codes it mobilizes extend as far as the eye can reach, they are indeterminable (...) ; the systems of meaning can take over this absolutely plural text, but their number is never closed, based as it is on the infinity of language.«

Like Barthes, Michel Foucault also understands the text as a network of connections. But he considers this network to be possible not only in the digital space, but also in the form of the printed book. In

he points out that the boundaries of a book are never clearly drawn because it is integrated into a system of references to other books, other texts and other sentences and thus functions as a node in a network of references. It is striking that structuralists and post-structuralists, such as Barthes and Foucault, describe the text, the world of letters and the power and status relations associated with it in terms that are also used in the field of computer hypertext.

»I evoke the term handmade web to refer to web pages coded by hand rather than by software; web pages made and maintained by individuals rather than by businesses or corporations; web pages which are provisional, temporary, or one-of-a-kind; web pages which challenge conventions of reading, writing, design, ownership, privacy, security, or identity.«

Graphical user interface (GUI) refers to a form of user interface on a computer. It has the function of making application software on a computer accessible by using graphic symbols, which are also called widgets. With computers, this is usually done by using a mouse as a control device with which the graphic elements are operated or selected; smartphones, tablets and other devices are usually operated by touching a sensor screen. The concept of the GUI became popular in 1984 with Apple's Macintosh, and developed into the industry standard for personal computers in the 1990s.

The GUI was decisively shaped by the engineers Douglas Engelbart and Alan Kay, who saw the potential of computers to be a visual experience similar to television. Inspired by the realism of these media, they developed not only the GUI in the 1960s, but also the computer mouse, which was from then on used for interaction and navigation within the interface. This turned the computer into a visual medium that enabled
applications and was no longer just a

Cascading Style Sheets or short CSS is a style-sheet language used for describing the presentation of a document written in a markup language such as

. CSS is a cornerstone technology of the World Wide Web, alongside HTML and JavaScript. CSS is designed to enable the separation of presentation and content, including layout, colors, and fonts. The term cascading derives from the specified priority scheme to determine which style rule applies if more than one rule matches a particular element. This cascading priority scheme is predictable.
In the first years after its development, the

vocabulary grew constantly. More and more visually distinguishing elements were added, such as big, small, centre or font. Although HTML is technically a language that distinguishes elements based on their content and not their presentation, it was more and more used as a visual design tool. Håkon Wium Lie, who was doing research at CERN at the same time as Tim Berners-Lee, therefore proposed a new format to describe the visual representation of an HTML document. This language, which he developed shortly afterwards together with the developer Bert Bos, he called Cascading Style Sheets.
